oil.summary: Crude staged a violent short-covering rally on July 8, with WTI closing at $74.76 (+6.13%) and Brent at $79.25 (+6.86%), both extending a weekly gain exceeding 7-8%. The catalyst is unambiguous: the U.S. launched airstrikes on Iran—hitting upwards of 80 targets per multiple reports—and revoked the sanctions waiver on Iranian oil after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Approximately 63 million barrels of Iranian crude are now stranded at sea, tightening available Atlantic Basin supply. Adding a second geopolitical shock, Ukraine struck eight Russian shadow-fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov, and Russia subsequently banned all diesel exports to protect its domestic fuel market following U.S.-intelligence-guided drone strikes on its refineries—explaining the extraordinary 13% surge in Heating Oil. A 3-million-barrel surprise EIA crude build provided a modest counter-signal but was overwhelmed by the geopolitical premium.
drivers: U.S. airstrikes on Iran and revocation of oil sanctions waiver locks ~63 mb of Iranian crude out of global markets and raises Strait of Hormuz disruption risk
Ukraine's strike on eight Russian shadow-fleet tankers plus Russia's retaliatory diesel export ban tightened distillate markets, sending Heating Oil up 13%
EIA reported a surprise +3.0 mb crude inventory build for the week ending July 3, a bearish datapoint that the market largely discounted against the geopolitical backdrop

gas.summary: The European and North American gas markets diverged sharply today. TTF surged 5.30% to €49.045/MWh—up nearly 13% on the week—likely tracking the broader energy risk premium generated by the Iran-Strait of Hormuz crisis and potential knock-on effects on LNG shipping routes, though no gas-specific headline directly explains the move in today's feed. Henry Hub slipped 1.44% to $3.218/MMBtu, continuing a mild week-on-week drift lower, with no material domestic supply or demand catalysts evident in the available headlines. The sole headline in the gas feed—Canada and Alberta signing an MOU on a West Coast oil pipeline—is not directly gas-relevant. Desk note: headline coverage for this sector is thin today; the TTF move warrants monitoring for LNG-route disruption news not yet captured.
drivers: TTF +5.3% on the day and +12.9% on the week, likely reflecting geopolitical risk spill-over from the Strait of Hormuz crisis and its potential impact on LNG shipping
Henry Hub eased 1.4% with no bullish domestic catalysts visible in today's news flow
Sector-specific headline coverage is limited; the Canada-Alberta West Coast pipeline MOU is oil-focused and not a near-term gas price driver

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs slipped 1.58% to $74.785, a modest pullback that sits within a broader one-month +3.98% uptrend. TTF's 5.3% jump is the dominant short-term input cost signal for European gas-fired generators. On the structural side, two notable longer-dated stories crossed the wire: global nuclear capacity is forecast to jump 44% by 2036, with China overtaking the U.S. as the largest nuclear power nation, and India is accelerating a $100 billion grid investment underpinning a solar manufacturing boom. A UK airline, Jet2, was reported to have turned the jet-fuel price surge into a ~£400 million hedging windfall. The Iran/Hormuz conflict headlines that dominated oil also appeared in this feed but are captured in the oil section. Overall, today's power and carbon data flow is thin on direct near-term price catalysts.
drivers: TTF's 5.3% daily spike raises European gas-fired generation costs, creating upward pressure on power prices despite the EUA dip
Global nuclear capacity projected to rise 44% by 2036 with China becoming the leading nuclear nation—a long-term bearish signal for carbon-intensive generation
India's $100 billion grid investment is accelerating solar manufacturing, pointing to sustained renewable capacity build-out in a major emerging demand centre
